batch_notes: Data quality: lipgloss's `readme` field is a sliding chunk of a markdown table, so the '(lipgloss/25)' cell attaches lipgloss/25 to bugs_direct/mentioned_by of nine properties that have nothing to do with Blend2D; only TestHegelBlend2DReachesBothEnds (and Blend1D) really concern it. Recurring shape the rubric does not name: lipgloss properties that detect a known bug and `count(...)`+return instead of failing (Blend2DReachesBothEnds, Place fractional positions, StyleRunes multi-line, Tree /14 /15 /21, ListEnumerators /17, Render cluster-torn) -- they are gated properties whose bug attribution is explicit but which can no longer fail on those bugs; Blend2DReachesBothEnds is effectively a pin that never fails. jsonparser is the mirror image: its nine bug-named tests are generative properties (tagged pin) with bugs_direct set, so it has no example pins and needs no attributions, while json-iterator (32 pins, 6 properties) has all its bugs on example tests; json-iterator properties cite pin test names rather than bug ids when gating, which I counted as explicit. Another shape between categories: 'generator-side model tree' tests (jsonparser) where documents are rendered from a tree and results compared to a lookup in it; I classified these model-oracle since the tree plus setPath/deletePath/lookup is a reference implementation, not just a constructed witness. Several semver/lipgloss parse or render properties also fold in 'many entry points agree' (StrictNewVersion/NewVersion/MustParse/JSON/Text/Scan; String()==Render()), an internal-consistency aspect with no tag in the rubric. Many inferred attributions in gojq and semver rest on generator coverage that is only described in the README, not visible in the 45-line bodies.
